description: Hi! I'm a Computer Science student with experience in Python, YOLO, OpenCV, machine learning and web application development. I'm currently working on LunarSafe AI, an AI-powered lunar landing site assessment concept. Looking for teammates with interests or skills in Data Analytics, GIS, Machine Learning, astronomy or UI/UX design who are passionate about building innovative solutions together!
summary:
LunarSafe AI is a mission-planning tool that tells you when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon at any site on the Moon, focusing on the lunar south pole. Future Artemis-era missions there depend on two things: sunlight for solar power and heat, and line of sight to Earth for direct communication. Both change constantly near the pole, where the Sun stays close to the horizon.

We built a Python engine that uses real NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE ephemeris kernels to compute Sun and Earth elevation over any UTC time window. It summarizes total sunlight, the longest darkness period, and Earth-contact windows. A web dashboard lets planners pick sites like Shackleton, Haworth, or Nobile crater rims, view interactive charts, compare several sites side by side, and export CSV data. And because it uses authoritative NASA geometry instead of simulated data, its output gives landing-site trade studies a reproducible baseline.
details:
What it does

LunarSafe AI computes the geometric elevation of the Sun and Earth above the local horizon at any lunar latitude/longitude over a chosen time window. From that time series it reports total sunlight hours, total Earth-visibility hours, the longest continuous sunlight and darkness periods, and every continuous visibility window.

How it works

Loads NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels: leapseconds (naif0012.tls), the DE440 planetary ephemeris (de440s.bsp), and lunar planetary constants (pck00011.tpc).

Converts each UTC sample to ephemeris time and gets the Sun and Earth position vectors relative to the Moon in the IAU_MOON frame.

Places the site on the Moon's reference ellipsoid and computes elevation from the angle between the line of sight and the local surface normal.

Aggregates samples into duration summaries and visibility periods.

Features

Command-line tool for single-time checks and batch time-series runs

Flask web dashboard with south-pole site presets (Shackleton, Haworth, Nobile rims) and custom coordinates

Interactive Plotly elevation charts with a 0° horizon line

Multi-site comparison scorecard

CSV export of full time series and summaries

Benefits and impact

South-pole missions face extreme lighting: long shadows, short sunlit windows, and intermittent Earth contact. The tool helps planners screen candidate landing sites and time windows early, using authoritative NASA geometry instead of approximations. Everything is open source and reproducible.

Tools and languages

Python, SpiceyPy (Python wrapper for NASA's SPICE toolkit), NumPy, Flask, Plotly, Tailwind CSS, HTML/CSS, pytest

Creativity

The tool turns professional-grade flight-dynamics data (SPICE) into a simple visual planner that a non-specialist can use in a browser. Both the CLI and the dashboard run on the same calculation engine, so results stay consistent.

Factors considered and limitations

We used geometric (not light-time-corrected) directions and treat the Sun and Earth as points at their centers. Terrain is not modeled yet, so crater walls and ridges that block the horizon are ignored. Next steps are adding a lunar elevation model (DEM/DSK) with ray-tracing for terrain shadowing, and higher-precision lunar orientation frames (MOON_PA/MOON_ME).
